terms.sub: Early Cardiogenesis and Heart Tube Formation
clues: The most cranial arterial outflow segment of the primitive embryonic heart tube.
It connects the bulbus cordis to the aortic sac and pharyngeal arch arteries.
Cardiac neural crest cells partition it via a spiral septum into the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.
The most caudal venous receiving chamber of the primitive embryonic heart tube.
It receives paired vitelline, umbilical, and common cardinal veins.
Its right horn is incorporated into the smooth wall of the right atrium, while its left horn becomes the coronary sinus.

terms.sub: Atrial Septation and Atrial Septal Defects
clues: A thin crescent-shaped membrane that grows downward from the roof of the common primitive atrium.
Its downward growth narrows the ostium primum toward the endocardial cushions.
Programmed cell death in its superior portion creates the ostium secundum before it forms the valve of the foramen ovale.
Specialized subendocardial mesenchymal swellings that develop in the dorsal and ventral walls of the atrioventricular canal.
They fuse in the midline during week 5 to divide the common AV canal into right and left orifices.
Failure of their fusion produces an atrioventricular septal defect strongly associated with Down syndrome.

terms.sub: Outflow Tract Septation and Conotruncal Anomalies
clues: A 180-degree spiraling partition formed by fusion of neural crest-populated truncal and bulbar ridges.
It divides the single embryonic outflow tract into two separate great arteries.
Failure of this partition to spiral results in transposition of the great arteries.

terms.sub: Outflow Tract Septation and Conotruncal Anomalies
clues: The most common cyanotic congenital heart defect presenting beyond the immediate neonatal period.
It results from anterosuperior displacement of the infundibular (conal) septum.
Its four classic components are pulmonary stenosis, VSD, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy.

terms.sub: Outflow Tract Septation and Conotruncal Anomalies
clues: A life-threatening cyanotic conotruncal malformation in which the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary trunk from the left.
It occurs when the aorticopulmonary septum takes a straight rather than a 180-degree spiral course.
Because systemic and pulmonary circuits run in parallel, neonatal survival requires an intracardiac or ductal shunt.
A congenital shelf-like constriction of the aortic lumen typically situated near the ligamentum arteriosum.
It produces upper-extremity hypertension with weak, delayed femoral pulses and is strongly associated with Turner syndrome.
Enlarged intercostal collateral vessels produce characteristic inferior rib notching on chest radiographs.
A pair of early embryonic vessels transporting nutrient-rich blood from the yolk sac to the sinus venosus.
Proliferating liver cords break up their proximal segments into the hepatic sinusoids.
Their anastomotic network around the duodenum forms the adult hepatic portal vein.
The main embryonic venous drainage system of the embryo proper, divided into anterior, posterior, sub-, and supracardinal pairs.
The right anterior and common vessels of this system form the adult superior vena cava.
The right subcardinal and supracardinal segments contribute to the adult inferior vena cava.
